lessons.title: What does a good workbook look like
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 1: What does a good workbook look like

theory.contentHtml:
A strong analysis workbook separates source data, calculations, and presentation so another person can audit it without breaking the source.

What to know

  • One row is one record; one column is one variable.
  • Keep merged cells, subtotals, and notes out of source tables.
  • Use meaningful sheet names: Raw, Clean, Analysis, Dashboard.

Worked example

One order belongs on exactly one row. OrderDate, CustomerID, Units, and Revenue are columns, not scattered blocks.

Quick check

If tomorrow's order can be added as one row without repairing formulas or layout, the structure is on the right track.

lessons.title: Data types are not display formats
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: Data types are not display formats

theory.contentHtml:
A cell that looks like a date or currency may still be stored as text. This causes many sorting, filtering, and calculation errors.

What to know

  • The underlying type determines what calculations are possible.
  • Formatting only changes how a value is displayed.
  • Use ISNUMBER, the status bar, and default alignment to spot type issues quickly.

Worked example

45000 can be formatted as currency while remaining the number 45000. The text '45000 looks similar but may be ignored by SUM.

Quick check

Switch from Currency to General. If the underlying value remains, that was formatting; if calculations still fail, inspect the data type.

lessons.title: Relative, absolute, and mixed references
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 4: Relative, absolute, and mixed references

theory.contentHtml:
The $ sign controls which part of a cell address stays fixed when a formula is copied - a small skill that affects an entire workbook.

What to know

  • A2 changes row and column.
  • $A$2 locks both row and column.
  • $A2 locks the column; A$2 locks the row.

Worked example

With a VAT rate in H1, use =F2*$H$1 so every copied row still points to the same rate.

Quick check

Press F4 while a reference is selected in a formula to cycle through all four locking modes.

lessons.title: Import CSV without corrupting data
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 7: Import CSV without corrupting data

theory.contentHtml:
Double-clicking a CSV lets Excel guess encoding, dates, and numbers. The import flow lets you control those decisions.

What to know

  • Use Data → From Text/CSV and verify UTF-8.
  • Keep leading-zero identifiers such as CustomerID as Text.
  • Do not overwrite the source; load into Raw or Power Query.

Worked example

If identifier 00124 is imported as a number it becomes 124; formatting later cannot restore the lost zeros.

Quick check

Before loading, inspect at least three columns: an ID, a date, and a decimal number.

lessons.title: Sort, filter, and data validation
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 9: Sort, filter, and data validation

theory.contentHtml:
Sorting and filtering help exploration; validation prevents new errors during data entry.

What to know

  • Sort the whole Table, never one detached column.
  • Use multi-level sorting when priorities matter.
  • Data Validation should include a clear input message and error alert.

Worked example

Sort Region A→Z, then NetRevenue Largest→Smallest to reveal the largest order in each region.

Quick check

After sorting, does each OrderID still match the correct CustomerID? If not, the sort detached columns.

lessons.title: Power Query repeatable cleaning
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 11: Power Query repeatable cleaning

theory.contentHtml:
If next month requires the same copy, split, trim, and type conversions, it is time for Power Query.

What to know

  • Every transformation is recorded and refreshable.
  • Set data types early, after confirming locale.
  • Name important steps by business meaning instead of leaving many Changed Type2 steps.

Worked example

One query can import the CSV, trim Region, parse OrderDate, remove duplicates, and load Clean with one Refresh All.

Quick check

Point the query to a newer file with the same schema and Refresh. If clean output updates without manual edits, the pipeline works.

lessons.title: SUM, AVERAGE, and descriptive statistics
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 14: SUM, AVERAGE, and descriptive statistics

theory.contentHtml:
Analysis starts with simple questions: total, average, spread, and the number of valid records.

What to know

  • Use COUNT for numbers and COUNTA for nonblank cells.
  • MEDIAN is less sensitive to outliers than AVERAGE.
  • MIN/MAX validate ranges and expose anomalies.

Worked example

If one 100-million order sits among many 1–3-million orders, AVERAGE is pulled upward while MEDIAN better represents a typical order.

Quick check

Always show count beside average; averages from 2 and 2,000 rows do not carry the same confidence.

lessons.title: SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, and AVERAGEIFS
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 16: SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, and AVERAGEIFS

theory.contentHtml:
The ...IFS functions answer conditional questions without manually filtering the table.

What to know

  • Place the sum/average range first, followed by criteria-range/criteria pairs.
  • All ranges must be the same size.
  • Build date criteria with an operator and cell reference, such as ">="&B1.

Worked example

=SUMIFS(tblSales[NetRevenue],tblSales[Region],A2,tblSales[Status],"Completed") calculates completed revenue by region.

Quick check

Change the Region in A2. The result should update without editing the formula.

lessons.title: Read and handle formula errors
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 18: Read and handle formula errors

theory.contentHtml:
Wrapping everything in IFERROR makes a workbook look clean but can hide bad data. Understand the error before handling it.

What to know

  • #N/A: not found; #VALUE!: wrong type; #DIV/0!: zero denominator.
  • Use Evaluate Formula and inspect each part.
  • Use IFERROR only for an expected error with a meaningful fallback.

Worked example

A conversion rate can use =IF(Visits=0,NA(),Orders/Visits) so a chart does not plot a misleading zero.

Quick check

If the fallback is an empty string, will downstream calculations ignore it? Verify before choosing the handling strategy.

lessons.title: IF, AND, OR, and business rules
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 22: IF, AND, OR, and business rules

theory.contentHtml:
Logical formulas turn verbal business rules into repeatable, testable conditions.

What to know

  • Write the rule as a sentence before writing IF.
  • Use AND when all conditions must hold; OR when any one is enough.
  • Avoid deeply nested IF; consider a mapping table or IFS.

Worked example

An order needs review if NetRevenue > 3 million or Discount > 10%: =IF(OR(...),"Review","OK").

Quick check

Build a four-case TRUE/FALSE table to verify AND/OR matches the rule.

lessons.title: XLOOKUP and INDEXMATCH
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 24: XLOOKUP and INDEXMATCH

theory.contentHtml:
A lookup connects an identifier to attributes in another table. XLOOKUP is clearer for common cases; INDEX/MATCH helps with compatibility or extra flexibility.

What to know

  • Lookup keys must be clean and of the same type in both tables.
  • Use exact match unless the business rule truly needs approximate match.
  • Do not hide every #N/A; expose Missing Key as a data-quality status.

Worked example

=XLOOKUP([@CustomerID],tblCustomers[CustomerID],tblCustomers[Segment],"Missing") enriches sales with customer Segment.

Quick check

Count Missing results. If greater than zero, inspect keys before continuing the analysis.

lessons.title: FILTER, UNIQUE, and SORT
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 26: FILTER, UNIQUE, and SORT

theory.contentHtml:
Dynamic arrays create self-expanding lists without copying formulas down every row.

What to know

  • UNIQUE creates dimension lists; SORT orders the result.
  • FILTER returns multiple rows matching a condition.
  • The spill area must be empty; place these formulas outside an Excel Table.

Worked example

=SORT(UNIQUE(tblSales[Product])) creates a product list that updates when the Table grows.

Quick check

Add a new product to the Table. Does the spill list expand without filling down?

lessons.title: Thinking in PivotTables
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 30: Thinking in PivotTables

theory.contentHtml:
A PivotTable translates a business question into four areas: Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters.

What to know

  • Dimensions go to Rows/Columns; measures go to Values.
  • Verify the aggregation: Sum, Count, or Average.
  • Refresh after source changes and prefer an Excel Table source.

Worked example

‘Revenue by region each month?’ becomes Rows: Month, Columns: Region, Values: Sum of NetRevenue.

Quick check

If Values shows Count of NetRevenue, check whether the source column is stored as text.

lessons.title: Choose charts by question
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 32: Choose charts by question

theory.contentHtml:
A good chart starts with the relationship to reveal, not a gallery of attractive chart types.

What to know

  • Compare categories with bars/columns; show time trends with lines.
  • For composition, prefer 100% bars or stacked charts; use pie only for very few groups.
  • Remove 3D, redundant legends, and distracting gridlines.

Worked example

Three months of regional revenue fit a line chart; quarterly totals for three regions fit a sorted bar chart.

Quick check

Hide the title and axes: can a viewer still infer the message in five seconds? If not, simplify the chart.

lessons.title: Design dashboards for decisions
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 37: Design dashboards for decisions

theory.contentHtml:
A dashboard is not a chart collection. It should help a specific audience answer a specific set of questions.

What to know

  • Top: KPIs; middle: trends and breakdowns; bottom: actionable detail.
  • Every chart needs a clear question and owner.
  • Use one color system with consistent spacing and alignment.

Worked example

A sales manager needs revenue, target, monthly trend, underperforming regions, and review orders - not 12 equally weighted charts.

Quick check

Write one action the dashboard supports. If you cannot, its scope is still too vague.

lessons.title: Hand off a workbook professionally
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 41: Hand off a workbook professionally

theory.contentHtml:
A workbook is only finished when another person can open, understand, refresh, and troubleshoot it without the author.

What to know

  • Remove unnecessary external links and verify source paths.
  • Distinguish inputs, formulas, and outputs with consistent styles.
  • Save a release version, keep a changelog, and avoid filenames like final_v2_new.

Worked example

Sales_Dashboard_2026Q1_v1.0.xlsx plus a README and changelog clearly communicates period, version, and usage.

Quick check

Close the workbook, reopen it on another machine or account, and run the handoff checklist exactly.
